package_info.package_versions: N/A (single malware suite, not versioned as a package)
package_info.why_malicious: HiddenWasp is a sophisticated Linux malware suite composed of a trojan, rootkit, and deployment script, engineered for covert remote control of infected systems. It enables attackers to execute arbitrary commands, download and run additional payloads, exfiltrate files, and maintain persistence, all while employing advanced evasion techniques to avoid detection by system administrators and security tools.

execution_context.file_location: trojan binary (custom ELF executable, typically dropped in /tmp or /var/tmp)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The trojan component receives remote commands, downloads and executes code, uploads files, and performs arbitrary shell commands on the infected system.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the trojan binary establishes a connection to a remote command and control server, receives and executes attacker-supplied commands, downloads and runs additional code, uploads files from the local filesystem to the attacker, and executes arbitrary shell commands, resulting in persistent, interactive remote access for the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code provides an attacker with persistent, interactive remote access and the ability to execute arbitrary commands, download and run additional payloads, and exfiltrate files, which are all hallmarks of backdoor malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Linux binaries do not open unauthorized remote command channels, execute arbitrary code from remote sources, or exfiltrate files without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools (RATs) in enterprise environments may provide similar functionality, but are installed with user consent, proper authentication, and are subject to monitoring.
key_indicators: Establishes outbound connections to attacker-controlled servers
Receives and executes arbitrary remote commands
Downloads and executes additional code at runtime
Uploads files from the victim system to remote locations
Operates as a background process with no user interaction

execution_context.file_location: rootkit module (kernel module or LD_PRELOAD library, typically loaded from /lib or /usr/lib, or injected via LD_PRELOAD)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The rootkit component hides files, processes, and network connections associated with the malware, preventing detection by system administrators and security tools.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the rootkit intercepts and manipulates system calls to hide the presence of malware-related files, processes, and network activity from system monitoring tools, enabling stealthy persistence and evasion of detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Rootkits are designed to conceal malicious activity and maintain persistence by hiding files, processes, and network connections, which is inherently malicious and intended to evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not attempt to hide its files, processes, or network connections from system monitoring tools or administrators.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some debugging, anti-cheat, or security software may use similar system call interception techniques, but only with user awareness, consent, and for legitimate purposes.
key_indicators: Hooks or intercepts system calls (e.g., open, readdir, netstat)
Hides specific files, directories, or processes from userland tools (e.g., ps, ls, netstat)
Requires root or kernel-level privileges for installation and operation
Loads unauthorized kernel modules or manipulates LD_PRELOAD

execution_context.file_location: initial deployment script (bash or shell script, typically executed from /tmp or downloaded and run directly)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The deployment script downloads the trojan and rootkit components, installs them on the system, and ensures persistence by modifying system startup scripts or services.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During initial infection, the deployment script downloads the trojan and rootkit binaries from remote servers, installs them to local directories, modifies system startup routines (such as /etc/rc.local, systemd service files, or crontab entries) to ensure persistence across reboots, and executes the malware components.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated download and installation of unauthorized binaries, combined with modification of system startup mechanisms for persistence, are classic signs of malicious installation scripts.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installation scripts do not fetch and install unauthorized binaries from untrusted sources or modify system startup for persistence without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System management scripts may automate software deployment and configure persistence, but only with user approval and using trusted sources.
key_indicators: Downloads binaries from remote, non-standard servers
Modifies /etc/rc.local, systemd service files, or crontab entries to establish persistence
Executes newly downloaded binaries with elevated privileges
Runs as a shell script, often from temporary directories

attack_chain.action: Initial deployment script downloads the trojan and rootkit components from remote servers, installs them on the system, and sets up persistence by modifying system startup scripts or services.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware components are installed on the system and configured to persist across reboots.

attack_chain.action: Rootkit component is loaded to hide the presence and activity of the malware, including files, processes, and network connections.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware remains concealed from system administrators and security tools, enabling stealthy operation.

attack_chain.action: Trojan component establishes a remote command and control channel, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary commands, download/upload files, and maintain full remote access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves persistent, covert remote control and can perform post-exploitation activities on the infected system.

behavioral_signatures: Installation or loading of unauthorized kernel modules or LD_PRELOAD libraries
Processes that conceal themselves or associated files from system monitoring tools (e.g., ps, ls, netstat)
Unusual outbound network connections initiated by binaries located in /tmp, /var/tmp, or user home directories
Persistence mechanisms involving unauthorized modifications to /etc/rc.local, systemd service files, or crontab entries
file_indicators: Unknown or suspicious ELF binaries present in /tmp, /var/tmp, or user home directories
Unauthorized kernel modules or shared libraries loaded at runtime (not matching known-good baselines)
Modified /etc/rc.local, systemd service files, or crontab entries referencing unknown binaries or scripts
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known HiddenWasp C2 IP addresses or domains (as identified in threat intelligence IOCs)
Unusual network traffic patterns originating from non-standard system processes or binaries in temporary directories
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized kernel modules and LD_PRELOAD libraries being loaded, and for hidden processes or files using system integrity and rootkit detection tools. Employ file integrity monitoring to detect new or modified binaries in sensitive or temporary locations. Audit system startup scripts and service files for unauthorized modifications. Analyze outbound network connections for links to known HiddenWasp C2 infrastructure using threat intelligence IOCs. Deploy YARA rules and behavioral analytics to identify HiddenWasp components and activity.
